title: Suri and the Shy Pumpkin Flowers
markdown:
In the sunniest patch of Farmer McGregor’s garden, next to the giggling tomatoes, lived Suri the squirrel. Suri was nuts about pumpkins. Her tail did a happy wiggle at their round cheerful bellies, their orange faces, and the way they smelled like warm autumn after rain.

But oh dear, the bright yellow pumpkin flowers were being shy. They opened for a blink, a quick peek at the world, and then snap—shut like tiny golden doors. No teeny pumpkins. No toasted seeds for the autumn feast.

Open, please, pretty flowers, Suri whispered, as she had whispered yesterday, and the day before.

Her whiskers twitched. Her paws darted from vine to vine. A tight knot sat in her tummy. She even tickled the petals with her whiskers, then blew a tiny puff, then waited with her paws folded like a very small farmer. One flower opened a golden eye, seemed to consider her, and shut. The others stayed closed, as if playing a very serious game of hide-and-seek with the sun. Her fluffy tail looped like a question mark. “How will we have pumpkins if the flowers won’t even try? How will I toast the seeds?” The worry felt bumpy, like a tiny unripe pumpkin of its own. A giggling tomato, unhelpful, wobbled next door.

A little whirring zipped past her ear. Zzzzzzt. Moss the beetle landed, shell shiny as a polished emerald. He was always busy, not wringing his small legs over pumpkins, but flitting from blossom to blossom, exploring every petal.

Suri’s voice came out sharper than she meant. “Moss. You’re always visiting flowers. Why aren’t you worried about the pumpkins?”

Moss settled on a daisy, legs tickling the white petals. “Worried? Why would I be worried, Suri? Look at me. See what I’ve got.”

Suri tilted her head. “You’ve got yellow fuzz. Does it make you itchy?”

Moss chuckled, tiny bells. “It is good. And see this?”

He flew first to a daisy, then to a big sunny pumpkin flower just starting to unfurl. He wiggled inside, legs busy. Tiny golden grains stuck to his fuzzy legs like sticky sprinkles. Then he flew to the next pumpkin flower along the same vine, and a few of those sprinkles fell off, dusting the new petals. It was a sparkly trail of sunshine, flower to flower. Suri followed on the ground, nose up, trying not to sneeze.

Open, please, pretty flowers, she thought again, and this time she watched instead of tickling.

After Moss had wiggled in one pumpkin flower and visited another, the flower he had left did not snap shut so fast. At its base, where blossom met stem, it looked a little rounder. Suri’s worry shrank. Curiosity fizzed up in its place.

“Moss, what is happening? The flowers aren’t closing right away. I think one of them is growing.”

Moss landed on a broad pumpkin leaf and did a happy tap-dance. “It is like a secret message service. This yellow dust is pollen. When I visit a flower, I pick some up. It sticks. When I visit another, I drop some off. A hug from flower to flower. When the flowers get enough pollen-hugs, they know it is time to grow into pumpkins.”

He wiggled his antennae. “Not only pumpkins. Apples. Berries. So many yummy things. That job is called pollination. Even small bugs matter. We explore all the beautiful flowers while we do it.”

Suri’s eyes went wide. A giggle rose. “You and your friends are little pollen-postmen? The flowers needed their mail so they could make pumpkins?”

“Exactly.” Moss looped in the air. “Now a tall sunflower is calling. Lots more pollen to deliver. Farewell for now.” And with a happy zzzzzzt he zipped away, a green blur toward the sky.

Suri watched him go, a warm pumpkin-y feeling all through her. Open, please, pretty flowers, she said one last time, and a few of them, dusty with Moss’s mail, stayed open long enough to mean it. The garden was full of busy secrets. She could not wait to see what other clever, helpful work was humming in plain sight, from one blossom to the next.
